caseNote: 가상 사례 (청소 서비스, 사내 HR팀) · 모든 수치는 설명용 + 실제 기업 (Facebook 초기 확장) 짧은 언급
insight: 첫 시장은 크기가 아니라 내가 얼마나 확실히 이길 수 있는지, 그리고 그다음 시장으로 이어지는지로 고른다.
misconception: 시장이 클수록 기회도 크니, 처음부터 최대한 넓은 고객을 노려야 한다.

sources.text: Moore, G. A. (1991). Crossing the Chasm. HarperBusiness. (beachhead/D-Day 비유)
Facebook 초기 확장 경로 (2004 하버드 → 다른 대학 → 2006 일반 공개), 회사 공식 연혁
청소 서비스와 HR팀 사례의 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 점유율 계산: 도시 전체 40 ÷ 200,000가구 = 0.02%. 단기임대 호스트 40 ÷ 150명 = 26.7% (카드에는 약 27%).
이동 시간 계산: 청소원 1명이 하루 4건, 이동 4회 가정. 도시 전체 4 × 35분 = 140분, 집중 지역 4 × 10분 = 40분, 차이 100분/일. 100분 × 3명 × 5일 = 1,500분 = 주 25시간. 2시간짜리 작업 기준 약 12건(25 ÷ 2 = 12.5).
Moore의 Crossing the Chasm(1991)이 D-Day 상륙 비유로 beachhead 개념을 설명한 점을 게시 전 원문으로 확인하세요. 같은 유닛의 STR-08-06과 겹치지 않도록 캐즘 개념 자체는 다루지 않았습니다.
Facebook: 2004년 2월 하버드 학생 대상 출시, 이후 다른 대학과 고등학교로 확장, 2006년 9월 13세 이상 일반 공개. 게시 전 공식 연혁으로 날짜를 확인하세요.

cards.title: Why 150 possible customers can beat 200,000
body: Maya is starting a home cleaning business with three cleaners and $3,000 for marketing. Her city has about 200,000 households.
One neighborhood has about 150 people who rent out apartments to short-term guests. On paper, that market is more than a thousand times smaller. The numbers say it may be the better place to start.

image.label: A city map with one small neighborhood glowing
image.brief: 따뜻한 플랫 일러스트. 넓은 도시 지도 전체는 회색, 한 동네만 밝은 색으로 빛나고 그 안에 작은 집 아이콘이 촘촘히 모여 있음. 청소 도구를 든 작은 인물 세 명. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Where should Maya spend her first $3,000?
body: She can only afford one real push in her first three months. Each option would likely bring in about 40 regular customers.
Which start gives her business the strongest footing?

options.text: Ads across the whole city. More households means more chances
options.feedback: She reaches the most people, but her 40 customers end up scattered, unconnected and far apart. The big market buys reach, not a foothold.

options.text: Target short-term rental hosts in one neighborhood
options.feedback: She gives up a huge audience but gains customers who are close together, need the same thing every week and talk to each other. The next card shows what that's worth.

options.text: Split it: half citywide, half on the hosts
options.feedback: It feels safe, but half a budget may be too little to win either group. She risks being a small name everywhere.

cards.title: Same 40 customers. Very different businesses.
body: Each cleaner does four jobs a day. Across the city, the drive between jobs averages 35 minutes. In one neighborhood, it's about 10. For three cleaners over a five-day week, that's **25 hours** of driving turned into time for about 12 more jobs.

breakdown.label: Citywide share
breakdown.detail: 40 of 200,000 households. Nobody has heard of her.

breakdown.label: Share of local hosts
breakdown.detail: 40 of 150. Most hosts know someone who uses her.

breakdown.label: Minutes driving per cleaner, per day
breakdown.detail: Scattered jobs vs jobs a few streets apart

breakdown.label: Paid time won back each week

cards.title: The beachhead market
body: A **beachhead market** is a small, clearly defined group of customers you set out to win first, and win almost completely, before moving on.
The name comes from a military landing: take one stretch of beach, secure it, then push inland. Geoffrey Moore used this picture in his 1991 book *Crossing the Chasm*.
The point isn't to stay small. It's to become the obvious choice somewhere, so you have a base to grow from.

image.label: One flag planted on a small beach, arrows pointing inland
image.brief: 단순한 인포그래픽. 해안선의 작은 구역 하나에 깃발이 꽂혀 있고, 그 뒤로 "Next segment" 라벨이 붙은 화살표 두세 개가 내륙으로 뻗음. 군사적 느낌보다는 지도 같은 차분한 톤. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: What makes a good beachhead
list: **Same need:** every host needs a fast clean between guests, so one offer fits all
**They talk:** hosts share tips, so each happy customer brings referrals
**Cheap to reach:** one neighborhood, one message, short drives
**Somewhere to go next:** nearby segments can use the same skills and reputation
cards.callout: Small is not the goal. Winnable is.
cards.softwareNote: Facebook launched in 2004 only for Harvard students, then opened to other colleges, and only later to everyone. Each campus was dense enough that joining made sense because your friends were already there.

cards.title: The beachhead points to the next beach.
body: Once Maya owns the hosts, her next step is close by: property managers in the same neighborhood who need move-out cleans. Same streets, same skills, and the hosts can vouch for her.
After that come regular homeowners nearby. Each step reuses routes, staff and reputation she already has.
A citywide start would have given her none of that. She'd be fighting for every customer from zero.

cards.title: A beachhead can also be a dead end.
body: Too small, and the segment can't support the business. If there were only 15 hosts, owning all of them still wouldn't pay three cleaners.
Too isolated, and it leads nowhere. A niche whose skills and reputation don't carry over to anyone else is a trap, not a base.
And focus has a cost: you'll say no to customers outside it for a while. That only pays off if you truly dominate the group you chose.

cards.title: Now you're rolling out a new process at work.
body: You lead a small HR team. You've built a new onboarding process for new hires, and you want all 12 departments in your company to use it. You have time to support only a few teams closely.

options.text: Launch to all 12 departments at once with a training video
options.feedback: Everyone hears about it, but nobody gets enough help to make it stick. Early confusion can turn the whole company against it.

options.text: Start with the department that hires the most and struggles most with onboarding
options.feedback: Their pain is real and their results will be visible. Win them fully, and their managers become your proof for the next teams.

options.text: Start with the smallest, friendliest department because it will be easy
options.feedback: Easy to win, but a team that rarely hires won't show results anyone notices. It's a beach that leads nowhere.

cards.title: Win one group completely before chasing everyone.
body: A small market you can dominate often beats a big one where you're invisible. Pick a group with the same need, that talks to each other, that you can reach cheaply, and that leads somewhere next.
**Try it today:** name the one group of customers where you could become the obvious choice. Then name the group you'd win next.
